visualTexts.title: School Bus Fare Revision
visualTexts.html:
RIVERBANK PRIMARYFROM 1 JANUARY
School bus fares
Monthly fare, payable by the 5th of each month
ZoneDistanceOne wayBoth ways
AUnder 2 km$42$70
B2 – 4 km$50$84
COver 4 km$58$96
Please read before paying
Families with two or more children on the bus pay full price for the eldest and half price for each younger child.
Pupils in Zone A who live within 700 m of the school are not eligible for the bus.
There is no refund for days missed, but a month may be skipped if the office is told before the 25th of the previous month.
Pay at the general office or by PayNow to UEN 198900123R. Enquiries: 6555 0930.

questions.q: How much does one child in Zone B pay for both ways each month?
questions.tip: Read across the Zone B row to the "Both ways" column, which gives $84.

questions.q: A family lives 5 km away and sends two children both ways. What is the monthly total?
questions.tip: $96 full for the eldest plus $48 half price for the younger.

questions.q: A pupil lives 500 m from the school. What does the notice say?
options: She is not allowed to take the bus
questions.tip: The shaded box says "Pupils in Zone A who live within 700 m of the school are not eligible".

questions.q: A pupil is absent for a week in March. What happens to the fare?
questions.tip: The shaded box says "There is no refund for days missed", so a week's absence changes nothing.

questions.q: A family wants to skip June. By when must they tell the office?
questions.tip: The notice says the office must be told BEFORE the 25th of the previous month, so the last day is 24 May.

questions.q: When is each month's fare due?
questions.tip: The line under the heading says the monthly fare is "payable by the 5th of each month".

questions.q: Why does the notice say "Please read before paying" above the shaded box?
options: The box is the least important part
To stop families paying the wrong amount
questions.tip: The heading warns families to read the sibling half-price and eligibility rules first, so they do not pay the wrong amount.

questions.q: A family with three children in Zone A, all travelling both ways, pays how much?
questions.tip: $70 full plus $35 and $35 half price.

visualTexts.title: Screen Time by Age Group
visualTexts.html:
HEALTH PROMOTION BOARD · ANNUAL SURVEY
Daily recreational screen time
Hours per day, excluding schoolwork
Survey of 4,200 households. Figures are self-reported by parents and previous studies suggest parents underestimate by roughly 20%.

Children with a screen in the bedroom averaged 1.6 hours more per day than those without, in every age group.

questions.q: Which age group is closest to the recommended limit?
questions.tip: The 4–6 bar is 1.3 hours, only 0.7 below the dashed "recommended limit 2h" line — the smallest gap.

questions.q: How much more screen time does the 10–12 group have than the 7–9 group?
By how much does the 13–15 group exceed the recommended limit?
questions.tip: The 13–15 bar reads 5.0 hours, and 5.0 − 2 = 3 hours above the dashed limit line.

questions.q: Why might the real figures be higher than the chart shows?
options: Parents tend to underestimate by about 20%
The chart is out of date
questions.tip: The note below says figures are "self-reported by parents" who "underestimate by roughly 20%".

questions.q: If the 20% underestimate is correct, roughly what is the true figure for the 10–12 group?
questions.tip: 4.2 plus about 20% is roughly 5.0.

questions.q: What does the survey say about screens in bedrooms?
options: They add about 1.6 hours a day in every age group
questions.tip: The last line says children with a bedroom screen averaged "1.6 hours more" daily "in every age group".

questions.q: Mei Ling says the chart proves that a child's screen time goes up as that child gets older. Why is she wrong?
options: The chart compares four different age groups at one moment; it does not follow the same children as they grow
The chart does not show screen time at all
The bars are drawn to the wrong scale
questions.m: The chart compares four different age groups at one moment; it does not follow the same children as they grow
a: The chart compares four different age groups at one moment; it does not follow the same children as they grow
questions.tip: A snapshot of different groups is not the same as following one group over time.

questions.q: Using the chart and the note at the bottom, roughly how many hours a day would a 13- to 15-year-old with a screen in the bedroom be likely to average?
questions.tip: The 13–15 bar reads 5.0 hours, and the note adds about 1.6 hours for a bedroom screen.

questions.q: Where is the lost property box?
questions.tip: The line under the heading says "The lost property box is outside the general office".

questions.q: When can a pupil look in the box?
questions.tip: The Open row of the table says "Recess and after school".

questions.q: A pupil has lost her water bottle. Where should she look?
options: On the blue rack by the canteen
questions.tip: The "Not kept in the box" panel says water bottles "are washed and put on the blue rack by the canteen".

questions.q: A pupil has lost his watch. What should he do?
options: Ask Mrs Selvam inside the office
questions.tip: The same panel says watches and anything valuable are kept inside the office — "ask Mrs Selvam".

questions.q: What happens to a lunchbox left behind on Monday?
options: It is kept for four weeks
It is thrown away that day
It goes on the blue rack
questions.tip: A lunchbox is a food container, and the panel says those "are thrown away at the end of each day".

questions.q: What happens to items nobody collects?
options: They are thrown away after a week
They are kept for four weeks, then given away
They are returned to the classroom
questions.tip: The "Kept for" row says items stay "4 weeks, then donated".

questions.q: Why does the notice say to write your name on the inside?
options: So the name does not rub off
Because the outside is too small
questions.tip: The tip says "permanent marker, on the inside" — the notice wants a lasting mark, and inside surfaces are rubbed less.

questions.q: Who is this notice written for?
questions.tip: The table tells the reader to bring "Your name and class", so it is speaking directly to children in the school.

questions.q: Which camp runs for more hours in total?
questions.tip: Adventure is 8.5 hours a day; Maker is 4.

questions.q: A nine-year-old wants to join Adventure Camp. What is the problem?
options: He is below the minimum age
questions.tip: The Ages row gives 10–14 for Adventure Camp, so a nine-year-old is a year too young.

questions.q: On which days do the two camps overlap?
questions.tip: Adventure Camp runs 8–12 Dec and Maker Camp 10–14 Dec, so the shared days are 10, 11 and 12 December.

questions.q: A family sends two children to Maker Camp. What is the total fee, before deposits?
questions.tip: $150 plus $127.50 after the 15% sibling discount.

questions.q: What happens to the $20 paid by Maker Camp participants?
options: It is kept by the centre
It is returned if no tools are damaged
questions.tip: The "Before you choose" box calls it a materials deposit "that is returned if no tools are damaged".

questions.q: Adventure Camp is cancelled because of a red weather warning. What happens?
questions.tip: The box says Adventure Camp is cancelled for a red weather warning and "fees are refunded in full".

questions.q: Why is Maker Camp more likely to fill up quickly?
options: It is cheaper and has only 16 places
questions.tip: Its fee is $150 against $220, it has only 16 places, and places go "in order of registration".

questions.q: A parent needs a camp that covers the whole working day and includes a meal. Which should she choose, and why?
options: Maker Camp, because it is cheaper
Adventure Camp, because it runs 8.30 to 5 and includes lunch
questions.tip: The Times row gives 8.30 a.m. – 5 p.m. and the Fee row says "$220 (lunch included)".

listening4.title: Listening Comprehension · Practice Paper 4
listening4.instructions: An adult reads each text aloud TWICE at a normal pace, with a short pause between the two readings. The child reads the question and the four options first. Do not show the child the script. 20 marks.

items.script: Good morning. A reminder that the school photograph will be taken tomorrow during the second period. Pupils should wear their full school uniform, including the tie. Those with physical education in the morning should bring their PE attire to change into afterwards, not before.
items.q: What must pupils do differently tomorrow?
options: Change into PE attire after the photograph

items.script: Boy: Did you finish the poster? Girl: Almost. I need one more photograph but the printer is out of colour ink. Boy: My father has a colour printer. Girl: Could you print it tonight? I'll send you the file now.
items.q: What will the boy do?

items.script: Attention, library users. The self-return machine on level one is out of service until Thursday. Please return books at the counter instead. Items returned to the counter are processed on the same day, so there is no risk of a late fine.
items.q: Why is there no risk of a fine?
options: Counter returns are processed the same day

items.script: Girl: How was the audition? Boy: I got in, but for the chorus, not the part I wanted. Girl: That's still good. Boy: I know. I'm trying to be pleased about it and mostly succeeding.
items.q: How does the boy feel?

items.script: For this experiment you will need a clear glass, water, and a coin. Place the coin under the glass, not inside it. Look through the side of the glass and the coin will appear to vanish. Pour the water in slowly and it will reappear. The water changes how light bends as it passes through.
items.q: Where should the coin be placed?

items.script: Woman: I'd like to change this shirt for a larger size. Assistant: Certainly. Do you have the receipt? Woman: Yes, here. Assistant: The larger size is out of stock in this colour, but we have it in navy, or I can order the same colour for Friday.
items.q: What are the woman's two options?
options: A refund or a credit note
Navy now, or the same colour on Friday
Wait a month or pay more

items.script: Residents are reminded that the swimming pool will be closed from Monday to Wednesday next week for its annual cleaning. The gym and the function room remain open as usual. We apologise for the inconvenience and thank residents for their understanding.
items.q: What remains open?
options: The gym and the function room

items.script: Boy: Why are you carrying two bags? Girl: One is my sister's. She sprained her wrist at training yesterday. Boy: Is it serious? Girl: Not really, but she can't carry anything heavy for two weeks, so I'm the donkey until then.
items.q: Why is the girl carrying two bags?
options: Her sister cannot carry anything heavy

items.script: Today's travel news. Engineering works mean there will be no train service between Sengkang and Punggol this Sunday. Free shuttle buses will run every ten minutes from both stations. Journey times will be about fifteen minutes longer than usual, so passengers should allow extra time.
items.q: What should passengers do on Sunday?
options: Take the free shuttle bus and allow extra time

items.script: Girl: I've decided to stop the piano. Father: After six years? Girl: I don't enjoy it any more. Father: All right. But finish the grade you've paid for, then decide. If you still want to stop in March, we'll stop.
items.q: What does the father suggest?
options: That she finishes the current grade, then decides
That she must continue for six more years

items.script:
Right, everyone, settle down. This is the briefing for the Primary Five science trip to the wetland reserve.

We leave from the school gate at eight sharp on Thursday. The coach will not wait. If you are late, your parents will have to bring you, and the reserve is forty minutes away by car.

Wear closed shoes. Not sandals, not slippers — closed shoes. Some of the boardwalk is wet and there are mangrove roots underneath it. Bring a hat, a refillable water bottle and your field notebook.

Do not bring food. This is not about tidiness. The reserve has a resident population of long-tailed macaques, and a monkey that has been fed once will approach the next group of children it sees. Last year a pupil from another school had a bag taken straight off her shoulder.

At the reserve you will be in groups of six with one parent volunteer each. Stay with your group. If you become separated, do not go looking — stop where you are and wait, and somebody will come back for you within a few minutes.

Finally, your notebooks. You are recording three things at each of the four stations: what you can see, what you can hear, and one question you would like answered. The questions are the part I care about most. There are no marks for neat handwriting.
items.q: What time does the coach leave?
Why must pupils wear closed shoes?
options: The boardwalk is wet and has mangrove roots beneath it
Sandals are not allowed on the coach

items.q: Why is food forbidden?
options: Because monkeys that have been fed will approach children
There is a shop at the reserve

items.q: What should a pupil do if she gets separated from her group?
options: Stay where she is and wait

items.q: Which part of the notebook does the teacher care about most?

items.script:
Interviewer: You have been a swimming coach for thirty-four years. What have you changed your mind about?

Coach Devi: Quite a lot. When I started, I believed that the child who wanted it most would win. I was completely wrong.

Interviewer: Wrong how?

Coach Devi: Wanting it is not rare. Nearly every child in that pool at six in the morning wants it. What is rare is being able to lose a race on Saturday and still be in the water on Monday. That is the thing I cannot teach, and it is the thing that decides almost everything.

Interviewer: Can you spot it early?

Coach Devi: Not from the swimming. I watch what happens in the ten minutes after a bad race. Some of them want to be told it was not their fault. A few go and look at the board to see the actual time. Those are the ones.

Interviewer: What do you say to a child who has just swum badly?

Coach Devi: As little as possible on the day. They are not able to hear it. I tell them one specific thing that was good, because there is always one, and then I leave them alone. We talk properly on Monday.

Interviewer: And the parents?

Coach Devi: The parents are usually harder than the children. A parent who says nothing in the car is worth more than any coach. I have told a great many of them that, and about half of them have listened.
items.q: How long has Coach Devi been coaching?
What did she used to believe, and now thinks is wrong?
options: That the child who wants it most will win

items.q: What does she now think is the rare quality?
options: Being able to return to training after losing

items.q: How does she identify that quality?
options: By watching what a child does in the ten minutes after a bad race

items.q: What does she mean by "A parent who says nothing in the car is worth more than any coach"?
options: Silence after a defeat helps a child more than analysis does
Parents should not speak to coaches
Cars are a bad place to talk
